concepts.title: Scheme gates: corpus, ticket size and investor count
concepts.hook: 20 crore corpus · 1 crore ticket (25 lakh insiders) · 1,000 investors · demat units.
concepts.tricky: Accredited investors are exempt from the minimum, not given a lower one.

concepts.title: Structure and tenure by category
concepts.hook: Cat I & II close-ended, 3 years minimum. Extension: 2 years, two-thirds BY VALUE.
concepts.tricky: The extension vote is by VALUE, not by number of unit holders.

concepts.title: Continuing interest of Manager and Sponsor
concepts.hook: 2.5% or 5 crore, whichever is LOWER — and never by waiving management fees.
concepts.tricky: Whichever is LOWER — on a large corpus the rupee cap binds, not the percentage.

concepts.title: Category III leverage and disclosure
concepts.hook: Leverage needs BOTH investor consent AND the Board's maximum limit.

concepts.title: Valuation and the Manager's responsibility
concepts.hook: Independent valuer computes it; the Manager still answers for it.
concepts.tricky: Appointing an independent valuer does not transfer responsibility for the result.

questions.concept: Scheme gates: corpus, ticket size and investor count
questions.question: The minimum corpus prescribed for each scheme of an AIF is:
questions.option_A: Twenty crore rupees, reduced to five crore for a social impact fund
questions.option_B: Twenty crore rupees for the fund as a whole, whatever its schemes
questions.option_C: Ten crore rupees per scheme, with no concession for any category
questions.option_D: Five crore rupees per scheme, raised to twenty crore for Category III
questions.correct_text: Twenty crore rupees, reduced to five crore for a social impact fund
questions.explanation: Reg. 10(b): each scheme shall have a corpus of at least twenty crore rupees, with the proviso reducing this to five crore for each scheme of a social impact fund. The test is per scheme, not per fund.

questions.concept: Scheme gates: corpus, ticket size and investor count
questions.question: An accredited investor proposes to commit fifty lakh rupees to a Category II scheme. The correct position is that:
questions.option_A: The commitment fails, because one crore is the floor for every investor
questions.option_B: The commitment is permissible, because the minimum does not apply to an accredited investor
questions.option_C: The commitment fails, because twenty-five lakh applies only to insiders
questions.option_D: The commitment is permissible only if the investor is also a director of the Manager
questions.correct_text: The commitment is permissible, because the minimum does not apply to an accredited investor
questions.explanation: The second proviso to Reg. 10(c) disapplies the minimum-investment clause altogether for an accredited investor. It is not a reduced threshold but an exemption from the clause.

questions.concept: Scheme gates: corpus, ticket size and investor count
questions.question: A scheme has 940 investors and proposes to admit 80 more, each investing two crore rupees. The compliance officer should identify that:
questions.option_A: The admissions are permissible, since each investor exceeds the one crore minimum
questions.option_B: The ceiling applies to the fund as a whole, so the scheme has ample headroom
questions.option_C: The admissions would breach the ceiling of one thousand investors for the scheme
questions.option_D: The admissions are permissible if the additional investors are all accredited
questions.correct_text: The admissions would breach the ceiling of one thousand investors for the scheme
questions.explanation: Reg. 10(f) caps a scheme at one thousand investors. Satisfying the ticket size does not cure a breach of the investor ceiling, and the cap is per scheme. Accreditation relaxes the minimum investment, not the count.

questions.concept: Scheme gates: corpus, ticket size and investor count
questions.question: State the four scheme-level gates and their figures.
A close-ended Category II fund seeks to extend its tenure. The requirement is approval of:
questions.option_A: A simple majority of the unit holders, counted by number of holders
questions.option_B: Three-fourths of the unit holders by value of their investment in the fund
questions.option_C: Two-thirds of the unit holders by number, with the Board's prior approval
questions.option_D: Two-thirds of the unit holders by value of their investment in the fund
questions.correct_text: Two-thirds of the unit holders by value of their investment in the fund
questions.explanation: Reg. 13(5): extension of up to two years requires approval of two-thirds of the unit holders BY VALUE of their investment. The vote is value-weighted, not a headcount.

questions.question: A sponsor proposes an open-ended Category II fund with a two-year tenure. The compliance officer should identify:
questions.option_A: Two defects — Category II must be close-ended and the tenure is below three years
questions.option_B: One defect — only the tenure, since Category II funds may be open-ended
questions.option_C: One defect — only the structure, since two years is a permissible tenure
questions.option_D: No defect, provided the tenure is fixed at the time of the application
questions.correct_text: Two defects — Category II must be close-ended and the tenure is below three years
questions.explanation: Reg. 13(1) requires Categories I and II to be close-ended, and Reg. 13(2) sets a minimum tenure of three years. Both limbs fail independently — the open-ended option belongs to Category III alone.

questions.question: Which categories may be open-ended, and what is the minimum tenure?

questions.concept: Continuing interest of Manager and Sponsor
questions.question: For a Category II AIF, the continuing interest of the Manager or Sponsor must be not less than:
questions.option_A: Five percent of the corpus or ten crore rupees, whichever is lower
questions.option_B: Two and a half percent of the corpus or five crore rupees, whichever is lower
questions.option_C: Two and a half percent of the corpus or five crore rupees, whichever is higher
questions.option_D: Five percent of the corpus, with no monetary cap applying to the figure
questions.correct_text: Two and a half percent of the corpus or five crore rupees, whichever is lower
questions.explanation: Reg. 10(d): 2.5% of corpus or five crore rupees, whichever is LOWER, for Categories I and II. The 5%/ten crore pair applies to Category III, and the test is the lower of the two, not the higher.

questions.concept: Continuing interest of Manager and Sponsor
questions.question: A Category III fund with a corpus of four hundred crore rupees proposes to meet its continuing interest by waiving management fees of twelve crore. The defect is that:
questions.option_A: The amount is short, since five percent of four hundred crore is twenty crore
questions.option_B: Category III funds are not subject to any continuing interest requirement at all
questions.option_C: The interest must be an actual investment and cannot be a waiver of management fees
questions.option_D: The waiver is permissible only if disclosed to investors in the placement memorandum
questions.correct_text: The interest must be an actual investment and cannot be a waiver of management fees
questions.explanation: Two points. The rupee cap means ten crore would satisfy the amount, since the test is the lower of 5% or ten crore. But Reg. 10(d) requires the interest to take the form of investment and expressly excludes a waiver of management fees, so the structure fails on form regardless of quantum.

questions.concept: Continuing interest of Manager and Sponsor
questions.question: State the continuing-interest figures for each category.
A Category III fund obtains investor consent and employs leverage within the specified limit, reporting only its overall leverage each quarter. The defect is that:
questions.option_A: Leverage requires the prior approval of the Board in addition to investor consent
questions.option_B: Category III funds may not employ leverage arising from derivative positions at all
questions.option_C: Reporting is required monthly rather than quarterly for any leveraged Category III fund
questions.option_D: The disclosure must break out cash borrowing, derivatives and the main source too
questions.correct_text: The disclosure must break out cash borrowing, derivatives and the main source too
questions.explanation: The proviso to Reg. 17(c) requires disclosure of the overall level of leverage, the level arising from borrowing of cash, the level arising from derivatives or complex products, and the main source — to investors and to the Board. An aggregate figure alone is incomplete.

questions.question: Leverage by a Category III AIF is permitted subject to:
questions.option_A: Consent from the investors and a maximum limit as specified by the Board
questions.option_B: The prior written approval of the Board for each borrowing transaction
questions.option_C: Consent of two-thirds of unit holders by value of their investment in the fund
questions.option_D: A maximum limit specified in the placement memorandum by the Manager
questions.correct_text: Consent from the investors and a maximum limit as specified by the Board
questions.explanation: Reg. 17(c): leverage or borrowing is subject to consent from the investors and to a maximum limit as may be specified by the Board. Transaction-by-transaction approval and the two-thirds-by-value test belong to other provisions.

questions.question: On what two conditions may a Category III AIF employ leverage?
Where established valuation policies would not produce a fair and appropriate valuation, the Manager:
questions.option_A: May continue applying the policy, provided the limitation is disclosed to investors
questions.option_B: Shall deviate from the policy, document the rationale, and report the deviation
questions.option_C: Must obtain the Board's prior approval before departing from the stated policy
questions.option_D: Shall refer the valuation to the trustee, whose determination is then final
questions.correct_text: Shall deviate from the policy, document the rationale, and report the deviation
questions.explanation: The provisos to Reg. 23 make deviation mandatory in that situation ('shall deviate'), coupled with documentation of the rationale and reporting of the deviation and its rationale to the trustee, board or designated partners and to investors.

questions.question: An AIF appoints an independent valuer who computes the portfolio value. Responsibility for true and fair valuation:
questions.option_A: Passes to the independent valuer once the appointment has been made
questions.option_B: Is shared between the Manager and the trustee in equal measure
questions.option_C: Remains with the Manager, notwithstanding the valuer's appointment
questions.option_D: Rests with the trustee, who must countersign the valuation report
questions.correct_text: Remains with the Manager, notwithstanding the valuer's appointment
questions.explanation: The Manager must ensure an independent valuer is appointed, but Reg. 23 separately makes the Manager responsible for true and fair valuation. Appointing a valuer discharges the appointment duty, not the responsibility for the outcome.

questions.question: Who performs the valuation, and who is responsible for it being true and fair?

lessons.concept: Scheme gates: corpus, ticket size and investor count
lessons.title: The four numbers that gate every AIF scheme
lessons.hook: Before strategy, before category, four numbers decide whether a scheme can exist at all: corpus, ticket size, investor count and the form units take. Get one wrong and the scheme is defective from launch.
lessons.cards: Twenty crore a scheme: LAW Each scheme of the Alternative Investment Fund shall have corpus of at least twenty crore rupees; each scheme of a social impact fund shall have a corpus of at least five crore rupees. | PLAIN The floor attaches to each SCHEME, not to the fund as a whole. A fund running three schemes must clear it three times. | WATCH The five-crore concession is confined to social impact funds. It is not a small-fund exemption. || One crore, with two carve-outs: LAW The AIF shall not accept from an investor an investment of value less than one crore rupees. Provided that for employees or directors of the AIF or of the Manager, the minimum shall be twenty five lakh rupees. Provided further that this clause shall not apply to an accredited investor. | PLAIN One crore is the general floor; twenty-five lakh for insiders; and the floor does not apply at all to an accredited investor. | WATCH The accredited-investor carve-out disapplies the clause entirely — it is not a reduced figure. || One thousand per scheme: LAW No scheme of the Alternative Investment Fund shall have more than one thousand investors. | PLAIN A per-scheme ceiling, counted scheme by scheme. | WATCH Where the AIF is formed as a company, the Companies Act, 2013 applies in addition. || Units in dematerialised form: LAW The Alternative Investment Fund shall issue units in dematerialised form subject to the conditions specified by the Board from time to time. | PLAIN Physical unit certificates are no longer the default position. | WATCH Inserted by amendment — a point where older material is out of date.
lessons.summary: Four gates per scheme: corpus twenty crore (five crore for a social impact fund); minimum investment one crore, twenty-five lakh for employees and directors, and disapplied entirely for an accredited investor; not more than one thousand investors; and units issued in dematerialised form.
lessons.tip: Check the four gates scheme by scheme, not fund by fund. The most common error in structuring is treating corpus and investor count as fund-level tests when the regulation applies them to each scheme.

lessons.title: Structure and tenure: what your category fixes for you
lessons.hook: Category is not just a label for your strategy. It decides whether your fund can be open-ended at all, and how long it may run.
lessons.cards: Close-ended by category: LAW Category I and Category II Alternative Investment Funds shall be close ended and the tenure of the fund or scheme shall be determined at the time of application. Schemes of Category III Alternative Investment Fund may be open ended or close ended. | PLAIN Categories I and II have no open-ended option. Only Category III schemes may choose. | WATCH Tenure is fixed at application for Categories I and II — not later. || Three years: LAW Category I and II Alternative Investment Funds or schemes launched by such funds shall have a minimum tenure of three years. | PLAIN A floor, not a default. Anything shorter cannot be registered. | WATCH The three-year floor attaches to Categories I and II; Category III is governed by its chosen structure. || Two years, two-thirds: LAW Extension of the tenure of the close ended Alternative Investment Fund may be permitted up to two years subject to approval of two-thirds of the unit holders by value of their investment in the Alternative Investment Fund. | PLAIN Up to two years, and only with a two-thirds vote measured by value. | WATCH By value, not by number of unit holders. Counting heads is the classic error.
lessons.summary: Categories I and II must be close-ended with tenure fixed at application and a minimum of three years; Category III schemes may be open- or close-ended; and a close-ended fund's tenure may be extended by up to two years with the approval of two-thirds of unit holders by value.
lessons.tip: Diarise the tenure end date at registration, not at first close. The two-thirds-by-value vote takes time to organise, and an expired tenure cannot be cured retrospectively.

lessons.concept: Continuing interest of Manager and Sponsor
lessons.title: Skin in the game: the continuing interest
lessons.hook: The regulation makes the Manager or Sponsor put money alongside the investors — and is precise about how much, and how it may not be provided.
lessons.cards: Lower of two figures: LAW Continuing interest in the Alternative Investment Fund of not less than two and half percent of the corpus or five crore rupees, whichever is lower, in the form of investment in the Alternative Investment Fund, and such interest shall not be through the waiver of management fees. Provided that for Category III Alternative Investment Fund, the continuing interest shall be not less than five percent of the corpus or ten crore rupees, whichever is lower. | PLAIN Categories I and II: 2.5% of corpus or five crore, whichever is LOWER. Category III: 5% or ten crore, whichever is lower. | WATCH Whichever is LOWER, not higher. On a large corpus the rupee cap binds, not the percentage. || Not by waiving fees: LAW …and such interest shall not be through the waiver of management fees. | PLAIN The interest must be a real investment. Foregoing fees does not count. | WATCH A fee waiver structured as economic exposure still fails this test. || Tell the investors: LAW The Manager or Sponsor shall disclose their investment in the Alternative Investment Fund to the investors of the Alternative Investment Fund. | PLAIN Holding the interest is not enough; it must be disclosed to investors. | WATCH Disclosure is a separate obligation from the holding itself.
lessons.summary: The Manager or Sponsor must hold a continuing interest of not less than 2.5% of corpus or five crore rupees, whichever is lower (5% or ten crore, whichever is lower, for Category III), by way of actual investment and not through any waiver of management fees, and must disclose that investment to investors.
lessons.tip: Compute both limbs at every close, since corpus moves. On a corpus above two hundred crore the rupee cap is what binds for Categories I and II — running the percentage alone will overstate the requirement.

lessons.title: Category III: leverage, and what it is conditioned on
lessons.hook: Category III is the only category that may employ leverage — but the permission is conditional, and the conditions are where compliance actually lives.
lessons.cards: Leverage, on consent and within a limit: LAW Category III Alternative Investment Funds may engage in leverage or borrow subject to consent from the investors in the fund and subject to a maximum limit, as may be specified by the Board. | PLAIN Two conditions attach: investor consent, and a maximum limit specified by the Board. | WATCH Consent alone is not enough, and neither is staying under the limit. Both must hold. || Four things to report: LAW Provided that such funds shall disclose information regarding the overall level of leverage employed, the level of leverage arising from borrowing of cash, the level of leverage arising from position held in derivatives or in any complex product, and the main source of leverage in their fund to the investors and to the Board periodically. | PLAIN Overall leverage, cash-borrowing leverage, derivative leverage and the main source — to investors and to the Board. | WATCH Aggregate leverage alone does not satisfy this; the composition must be broken out. || Regulated by direction: LAW Category III Alternative Investment Funds shall be regulated through issuance of directions regarding areas such as operational standards, conduct of business… | PLAIN Much of the Category III regime sits in directions rather than in the regulation text. | WATCH Reading the regulation alone will not give you the full Category III picture.
lessons.summary: Category III AIFs may engage in leverage or borrow, but only with investor consent and within a maximum limit specified by the Board, and must periodically disclose overall leverage, leverage from cash borrowing, leverage from derivatives or complex products, and the main source of leverage, both to investors and to the Board.
lessons.tip: Treat the leverage disclosure as four separate data points rather than one number. A report showing only aggregate leverage is incomplete on the face of the proviso.

lessons.title: Valuation: independent valuer, but the Manager owns the outcome
lessons.hook: The regulation splits valuation into two responsibilities that are easy to conflate: who performs it, and who is answerable for it.
lessons.cards: An independent valuer: LAW The Manager shall ensure that the Alternative Investment Fund appoints an independent valuer who satisfies the criteria specified by the Board from time to time. | PLAIN Appointment of an independent valuer is mandatory, on criteria the Board specifies. | WATCH An internal committee does not satisfy this. || The Manager, for true and fair value: LAW The Manager shall be responsible for true and fair valuation of the investments of the scheme of the Alternative Investment Fund. | PLAIN Delegating the computation does not transfer responsibility for the result. | WATCH An independent valuer's report is not a defence to an unfair valuation. || Depart, document, report: LAW Provided that in case the established policies and procedures of valuation do not result in fair and appropriate valuation, the Manager shall deviate from the established policies and procedures in order to value the assets at a fair value and document the rationale for such deviation: Provided further that such deviation and its rationale shall be reported to the trustee or the trustee company or the Board of Directors or designated partners and investors. | PLAIN Where policy produces an unfair result, the Manager must depart from it, document why, and report the departure. | WATCH Deviation is mandatory in that situation, not discretionary — 'shall deviate'.
lessons.summary: The Manager must ensure an independent valuer meeting the Board's criteria is appointed and that valuation is carried out as specified, while remaining responsible for true and fair valuation; where established policies would not produce a fair value the Manager shall deviate, document the rationale, and report the deviation and its rationale to the trustee, board or designated partners and to investors.
lessons.tip: Build the deviation trail before you need it: a dated rationale and a record of the report to the trustee and investors. The provision is drafted as an obligation to depart from policy, so silence when policy misprices is itself the breach.
